text: 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐃𝐚𝐯𝐚𝐨 𝐂𝐢𝐭𝐲 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐃𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐭  – 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐜𝐮𝐞 𝐅𝐨𝐫𝐜𝐞 (𝐃𝐂𝐅𝐃-𝐒𝐑𝐅) 𝐛𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐬 𝐒𝐰𝐢𝐟𝐭 𝐖𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐒𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐜𝐡 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐜𝐮𝐞 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐭𝐨 𝐁𝐮𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐮 𝐨𝐟 𝐅𝐢𝐫𝐞 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐋𝐮𝐳𝐨𝐧, 𝐛𝐞𝐜𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞 𝐩𝐫𝐞𝐩𝐚𝐫𝐞𝐝𝐧𝐞𝐬𝐬 𝐤𝐧𝐨𝐰𝐬 𝐧𝐨 𝐝𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞. Under the leadership of 𝐅𝐂𝐒𝐔𝐏𝐓 𝐑𝐈𝐙𝐀𝐋𝐃𝐄 𝐌 𝐂𝐀𝐒𝐓𝐑𝐎, Regional Director, and under the direct supervision of District Fire Marshal 𝐅𝐒𝐔𝐏𝐓 𝐃𝐎𝐍𝐀𝐋𝐃 𝐑 𝐂𝐎𝐍𝐂𝐄𝐏𝐂𝐈𝐎𝐍, headed by 𝐅𝐒𝐈𝐍𝐒𝐏 𝐑𝐄𝐎𝐌𝐀𝐑 𝐂 𝐁𝐔𝐂𝐀𝐎, the Davao City Fire District – Special Rescue Force (DCFD-SRF) successfully conducted the Swift Water Search and Rescue Training for personnel of the  Bureau of Fire Protection Central Luzon The training equipped participants with essential knowledge, techniques, and practical skills in 𝙎𝙬𝙞𝙛𝙩 𝙒𝙖𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙎𝙚𝙖𝙧𝙘𝙝 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙍𝙚𝙨𝙘𝙪𝙚 (𝙎𝙒𝙎𝘼𝙍), enhancing their preparedness and operational capability in responding to emergencies involving floods, swift currents, and other water-related incidents.  The activity was further strengthened through the participation of 𝘿𝙞𝙨𝙖𝙨𝙩𝙚𝙧 𝙍𝙞𝙨𝙠 𝙍𝙚𝙙𝙪𝙘𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣 𝙖𝙣𝙙 𝙈𝙖𝙣𝙖𝙜𝙚𝙢𝙚𝙣𝙩 (𝘿𝙍𝙍𝙈) 𝙥𝙚𝙧𝙨𝙤𝙣𝙣𝙚𝙡 from the 𝘾𝙞𝙩𝙮 𝙤𝙛 𝙋𝙖𝙡𝙖𝙮𝙖𝙣 and the 𝙈𝙪𝙣𝙞𝙘𝙞𝙥𝙖𝙡𝙞𝙩𝙮 𝙤𝙛 𝙏𝙖𝙡𝙖𝙫𝙚𝙧𝙖, whose involvement underscores the importance of inter-agency cooperation and community-based preparedness in disaster response and rescue operations. The Davao City Fire District – Special Rescue Force extends its sincere appreciation to 𝐅𝐒𝐒𝐔𝐏𝐓 𝐁𝐄𝐑𝐍𝐀𝐑𝐃 𝐓. 𝐑𝐎𝐒𝐄𝐓𝐄, DSC, Acting Regional Director, BFP Region 3, for the support and leadership extended toward the successful conduct of this capability-building initiative. Likewise, heartfelt appreciation is extended to the  Nueva Ecija Provincial Office BFP R3  for its invaluable cooperation and support, which contributed significantly to the successful conduct of this training. We sincerely acknowledge the Provincial Office and all its personnel whose dedication and active participation helped make this important training initiative a success. From Davao City to Central Luzon, this training serves as a reminder that preparedness knows no distance. Through knowledge-sharing, skills development, and strengthened inter-regional cooperation, we continue to build a more capable and responsive firefighting and rescue force. Congratulations to all the participants and training team for the successful completion of the Swift Water Search and Rescue Training!  One Mission. One Standard. One BFP. Prepared to Respond. Ready to Rescue.  #BFPRegionXI #BFPOnse #onseatonibay #DCFDSpecialRescueForce #Lingkod_ToServe #dcfd_srf_updates

"Kumpleto"? Kumpleto sa pangako, pero baha pa rin sa realidad.  Yung ganda ng billboard, pang-electoral campaign lang pala ang kaya nitong pigilan. Habang nagpapapogi sa poster, yung mga residente at pamilya, kinakailangang mag-sagwan sa baha. Abot na abot yung pera para sa project, pero marami pa ring nakalubog sa baha. Yung "baha ay aayusin" na slogan, mukhang hindi naman natupad kasi hanggang ngayon, yung mga tao sa Sampaloc at iba pang lugar, baha pa rin ang kinakaharap araw-araw. Hindi kakayanin ng pictorial ang totoong kahirapan ng mga tao. Aba, sa dami ba naman ng puting papel sa proyekto, baka dito pa pala sa billboard na nalunod napunta ang focus? Kawawa naman ang mga tao, lalo na sa gitna ng matinding pag-ulan. Total na direktang hampas kay Rep. Maceda at sa mga gustong magpapogi: Sa panahon ng krisis, ang pangako sa billboard ay parang paputok: maingay pero panandalian lang. Yung mga taong bumubuhay sa kanila, sila pa ang nagtitiis sa baha. Ano ba talaga ang iniutos ng "proyekto" na ito? Hindi ba't dapat respetuhin ang buhay at kaligtasan nila? Sa Rep. Edward Maceda, 'yung sinasabing 'complete' na flood control, dapat i-audit ang pondo. Hindi pwedeng 'basta tapos na' ang usapan kung hindi naman nararamdaman ng mga tao ang solusyon.  #FloodControlPH #Sampaloc #EdwardMaceda #CompletedFloodControl #BahaPH #RainPH #UrbanFlooding #PhilPolitics #AccountabilityPH #SampalocFlooding #ManilaFloods #FloodRisk #InfrastructurePH #MayPerangNasayang #PhotoForensics

Nung bata ako, akala ko normal lang ang baha. Kapag malakas ang ulan, may baha. Ganun lang. Pero habang tumatanda tayo, unti-unti nating naiintindihan na hindi dapat maging normal ang isang bagay dahil lamang sa paulit-ulit natin itong nararanasan. Oo, malakas ang ulan. Oo, bahagi ng ating klima ang Habagat. At hindi natin kayang pigilan ang pag-ulan. Pero kaya nating paghandaan. Kaya nating ayusin ang drainage. Protektahan ang mga daluyan ng tubig. Ayusin ang urban planning. Magpatupad ng pangmatagalang flood-control solutions. At higit sa lahat, bumuo ng sistemang hindi kailangang hintaying lumubog ang mga komunidad bago kumilos. Ilang taon na tayong natutong pumasok sa paaralan na may baha, pumasok sa trabaho na may baha, umuwi na may baha. Hanggang kailan natin sasabihing “ganyan talaga sa Pilipinas”? Dahil hindi normal na ang bawat malakas na ulan ay nangangahulugang mawawalan ng kabuhayan ang isang pamilya. Hindi normal na ang mga estudyante ay kailangang tumawid sa baha para makauwi. Hindi normal na isang araw ng matinding ulan ay sapat para maparalisa ang buhay ng isang buong lungsod. At hindi dapat maging normal ang paulit-ulit na paghihintay sa susunod na baha para muling pag-usapan ang parehong problema. May mga lugar sa Metro Manila na nakitaan na ng improvements matapos ang drainage upgrades, dredging, at pumping-station projects—patunay na may mga solusyong gumagana kapag may maayos na pagpaplano at pagpapatupad. Kaya may pananagutan ang bawat antas ng pamahalaan—mula sa mga LGU hanggang sa national government—na tiyaking ang mga planong ito ay naipapatupad, napapanatili, at tunay na nakatutulong sa mga komunidad. Ang accountability ay hindi lamang pagresponde kapag may baha. Ito ay paghahanda bago pa ito dumating. Kaya ang tanong ngayon ay hindi kung bakit umuulan. Ang tanong ay: Bakit taon-taon, parang tayo pa rin ang kailangang masanay sa baha? Hindi natin hinihingi ang imposibleng walang baha. Ang hinihingi natin ay isang Pilipinas na hindi basta sumusuko sa baha bilang bahagi ng buhay. Dahil ang baha ay maaaring bahagi ng panahon. Pero ang pagiging hindi handa ay hindi dapat maging bahagi ng sistema.  #MetroManilaFlood #flooding #floodcontrol #bahaph

Bicol on blue alert as Super Typhoon Rosal enters PAR By Connie Calipay LEGAZPI CITY – Bicol’s Regional Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Council (RDRRMC) placed the region under blue alert on Tuesday as Super Typhoon Rosal (international name Champi) entered the Philippine Area of Responsibility (PAR) at about 10:40 a.m. In Memorandum 60, series of 2026, RDRRMC Chairperson and Office of Civil Defense (OCD) - Bicol Director Bernardo Fortes Jr. directed regional response agencies and local disaster risk reduction and management councils to intensify preparations and closely monitor the weather disturbance's potential effects. Under the directive, concerned agencies must activate their Emergency Operations Centers (EOCs) around the clock, ensure the readiness of response teams and assets, and implement contingency plans based on anticipated hazards. Response clusters led by various agencies have also been activated, including the Department of Health (DOH); the Department of Social Welfare and Development (DSWD) for food and non-food items, camp coordination and camp management, and protection of internally displaced persons; the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT) for emergency telecommunications; the Philippine National Police (PNP) for law and order; the Department of Education (DepEd) for education; and the OCD for early recovery. Provincial, city, and municipal disaster risk reduction and management councils were likewise instructed to hold pre-disaster risk assessment meetings, activate their incident management teams, and prepare evacuation centers and resources for possible emergency operations. Fortes also directed them to advise residents in flood-, landslide-, and lahar-prone areas to prepare for possible evacuation. Coastal communities vulnerable to storm surges were urged to remain alert and heed local advisories. The memorandum also called for the immediate dissemination of weather bulletins and advisories to barangay disaster risk reduction and management committees and residents, as well as the prompt reporting of incidents to the RDRRMC Operations Center. Response agencies must ensure the availability of personnel and equipment for possible deployment, test communication systems with higher-level operations centers and barangay disaster response teams, and keep emergency hotlines updated on official websites and social media platforms. In its bulletin on Tuesday, the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) raised Wind Signal No. 1 over parts of Northern Luzon, including Batanes; the eastern portion of the Babuyan Islands, including Babuyan, Camiguin, and Didicas Islands; the eastern portion of mainland Cagayan; the northeastern portion of Isabela; and the northeastern portion of Catanduanes. Meanwhile, DSWD-Bicol Director Norman Laurio said he was overseeing preparedness, resource monitoring, and coordination to ensure timely assistance for affected Bicolano families. The regional social welfare office has prepositioned 410,158 family food packs (FFPs), 22,931 non-food items (NFIs), and 14,137 ready-to-eat food (RTEF) boxes in regional and local government unit warehouses to ensure timely assistance to affected families. SOUTHWEST FLASH FLOOD RISK WEDNESDAY AND THURSDAY an approaching storm system will bring rounds of heavy rain and thunderstorms to Southern California, Arizona and the Four Corners this week, with the flood threat expanding into New Mexico as the system moves inland. Unusually deep moisture will help fuel downpours capable of producing rapid runoff and localized flash flooding. Southern California’s concern increases Wednesday, especially Wednesday night into Thursday across Santa Barbara, Ventura and Los Angeles counties. Current forecasts favor roughly 0.5-2 inches, with locally higher totals beneath stronger storms. Brief rainfall rates near 0.75 inch per hour are possible, and a Flood Watch may become necessary. Farther south, Orange County, the Inland Empire and San Diego County will see their most active weather generally Wednesday night through Thursday afternoon. Around 1 inch is possible across Orange County’s coastal plain, with roughly 1.5 inches on favored mountain slopes. Across Arizona, there’s a risk of excessive rainfall for Phoenix and areas north and east on both days. Forecast totals across south-central Arizona generally range from 0.25-1 inch in the lower deserts to 1-2.5 inches in the higher terrain. Repeated thunderstorms could produce locally higher amounts, with showers becoming more widespread across southern Arizona Thursday. The flash flood threat also increases across northwestern New Mexico Wednesday, expanding toward the Rio Grande Valley late Thursday into Friday. Even fast-moving storms can cause flooding when multiple downpours cross the same locations. Burn scars, slot canyons, dry washes, arroyos and low-water crossings are especially vulnerable. Localized street flooding could also develop beneath heavier storms. Stay alert for warnings, reconsider canyon trips when storms are nearby, and NEVER drive through a flooded roadway

FLASHFLOOD EMERGENCY in Urban areas  Immediate Action: Stay Put and Signal If you are already stranded—whether on a roof, in a car, or on high ground—your primary goal is to wait for help. Do not attempt to travel through the floodwaters. 1. Get to the Highest & Safest Point  In a Building: Move immediately to the highest accessible floor. AVOID a closed attic. If the water continues to rise, you could become trapped without a way to escape. Only go onto the roof if absolutely necessary. If you do, have a way to break through (like an axe or shovel, if accessible) to prevent being trapped in an enclosed attic space. In a Vehicle: Do NOT drive through any floodwater. If your vehicle is surrounded by rapidly moving water: Stay in the vehicle unless the water is rising inside. If water is rising inside the vehicle, get out immediately and climb onto the roof. If you can, try to roll down windows early to equalize pressure and make the car less buoyant/more stable, then climb out. Outside on High Ground: Stay there. Do not attempt to cross or walk through any moving water. 2. Signal for Help  Rescuers must be able to see you, especially when the storm makes visibility low. Visibility: Use brightly colored clothing or fabric (red, orange, or reflective material) and wave it when you hear a helicopter or see a boat. Sound: Use a whistle (which can carry sound better than screaming) or bang on a metal object in a set pattern (like three short bangs). Light: Use a flashlight or the light on your phone to flash an SOS signal (three short, three long, three short flashes) at night or toward a distant search team. Communication: If you have a working mobile phone, call emergency services   Survival & Safety While Stranded 3. Manage the Hazards of the Water Floodwater is extremely dangerous, often called "black water." Contamination: Assume all floodwater is contaminated with sewage, chemicals, sharp debris (broken glass, metal), and potential biological hazards. Electrocution: Stay clear of downed power lines. Floodwater can become electrically charged. Do not touch any electrical equipment if you are wet or standing in water. Debris and Animals: Watch out for floating debris that can injure you. Snakes, insects, and other displaced animals may also be seeking refuge on your elevated spot. 4. Conserve Resources If you have your emergency kit with you: Water: Ration drinking water carefully. If you have absolutely no safe drinking water, you may need to use rainwater collection, but purification methods should be used if possible. Never drink floodwater. Power: Keep your phone powered off or in airplane mode unless actively communicating with rescuers or checking for official alerts. Food: Ration non-perishable food items. 5. Stay Alert and Monitor Conditions Official Alerts: Listen to a battery-powered or hand-crank radio for official announcements, evacuation orders, or changes in the storm path. Follow instructions from local emergency management immediately. Structural Integrity: If you are in a building, be alert for shifting noises, cracks, or signs of structural stress, especially if the wind and water are still severe.  Key Advice to Remember Do Not Enter Moving Water: Just 6 inches of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet. Do Not Attempt to Swim to Safety: The current, hidden debris, and contamination make this a last resort. Stay Warm and Dry: If possible, use blankets or dry clothes from your emergency bag to prevent hypothermia, which can happen even in warm climates due to wind and rain. Your single best defense now is to remain where you are (the highest point), stay visible, and wait for official rescue teams.

4 DPWH officials in Davao, Cebu sacked; Dizon says more heads to roll By Ferdinand Patinio MANILA – Four local officials of the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) in the cities of Davao and Cebu were sacked from their posts for various offenses. According to DPWH Secretary Vince Dizon, those that have been relieved from their posts effective Monday were Richard Ragasa, formerly assigned in Davao City; Lilibeth Sarmiento, assistant District Engineer; and Roberto Mamaril, head of the Construction Section. The three were among those recommended by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) for the filing of charges for violation of the Anti-Graft and Corruption Practices Act and Falsification by Public Officer in relation to flood control and other projects by the Genesis88 Construction in the said city. On the other hand, Renato Catingub, head of the Construction Section of the DPWH 4th Engineering District in Cebu, was sacked from his post based on the complaints lodged by contractors in the province. “Someone reported to me that a construction chief in Cebu is extorting money from contractors in Cebu,” Dizon said in an interview during the inspection of Diokno Pumping Station in Pasay City.  He noted that the relief of the four DPWH officials must serve as a stern warning that the department is serious in its campaign to bring back the trust and confidence of the people to the government. “To everyone in the DPWH: If you commit any wrongdoing or face charges, you will be automatically dismissed immediately,” Dizon said. “We are on a one-strike policy; once someone reports it, you are fired immediately,” he added. *More heads will roll* Dizon said he will be announcing or identifying erring DPWH personnel in the coming weeks as investigations are still ongoing. “There are ongoing investigations at the moment. I will make an announcement in the next few weeks involving District Engineers, Assistant District Engineers among others,” he said. “Officials at the regional and district offices are currently finalizing reports from the Legal Service and the Internal Audit Investigations Service. I will announce the names of those who will be removed in the coming months,” he added. *Coast Guard assistance* On the other hand, Dizon said they will seek the assistance of the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) to make sure that the several pumping stations along Roxas Blvd. are well-guarded amid the arrest of three individuals suspected to have stolen cable and electric component of the Diokno Pumping Station. “Regarding the six pumping stations here on Roxas Boulevard, we will deploy the Philippine Coast Guard—heavily armed Coast Guard personnel—along Roxas Boulevard to deter those lunatics who are planning to commit theft,” he said. The Secretary said he wants those arrested to do the work of its personnel, for them to experience how is it to collect trash, and clean esteros, which are being done by honest and hardworking men and women of the agency. “They should experience the hardships faced by our fellow citizens who earn an honest living—people who, despite their own struggles, would never resort to theft. Our President has repeatedly stated that we will not tolerate this kind of behavior,” Dizon said.  “It is a grave injustice, especially toward our honest, hardworking laborers—such as those at the DPWH, whose work is incredibly demanding—clearing away trash and cleaning out drainage systems. Yet, there are some unscrupulous individuals among us who just go ahead and steal, then sell what they’ve taken; that is simply unacceptable,” he said. (PNA) (Screengrab from DPWH video)

DAVAO: THE “FLOOD CAPITAL” — BUT PERHAPS NOT FOR THE REASON YOU THINK They say Davao is the “Flood Capital of the Philippines.” Well, if someone insists on giving us that crown, perhaps we should wear it proudly—but let’s first ask a simple question: What exactly is overflowing?  Yes, Davao experiences floods. We have rivers that swell after relentless rain, low-lying communities that sometimes bear the brunt of nature, sudden downpours that seem to arrive without an appointment, and roads that occasionally transform into temporary swimming pools. That is a real problem. It deserves real solutions—not political theater. But if we are going to compare cities, perhaps the scoreboard deserves more than a political slogan. During the severe southwest monsoon flooding in July 2025, for example, the Metropolitan Manila Development Authority reported hundreds of flooding incidents across Metro Manila within a single day. Ask someone where they came from, and you may discover an entire story behind the answer. Then, inevitably, there's food. Because in Davao, you can start a conversation about almost anything and somehow end up discussing durian.  “This variety is sweeter.” “No, that one has better texture.” “You haven't tried the best one yet.” Suddenly, what began as a casual conversation has transformed into an international conference on durian. No registration fee required.  But perhaps Davao's most remarkable flood is neither water nor culture. It is warmth. There is a quiet generosity in the character of many Dabawenyos that statistics cannot measure. You can arrive as a stranger and, before long, someone may already be telling you where to eat, what places to visit, which shortcut to take—and, most importantly, which road to avoid when traffic is terrible. That's not just hospitality. That's hospitality with a built-in traffic advisory.  And then there is Davao's natural beauty. The sea. Samal. Mount Apo. The forests. The farms. The rivers. The mountains. The wide spaces that remind you that progress and nature do not always have to be enemies. Davao is also changing. Businesses are arriving. Buildings are rising. Infrastructure is expanding. Communities are growing. People continue to come—not only because they are looking for jobs, but because they are looking for possibilities. Some arrive carrying résumés. Others arrive carrying business plans. Some arrive carrying nothing more than a dream. And somewhere along the way, many discover something unexpected: They don't merely live in Davao. They become part of it. That, perhaps, is the real story. A city should not be judged solely by the problems that rise within it. It should also be judged by what its people continue to build despite those problems. Davao is not perfect. We have traffic. We have growing pains. We have environmental concerns. We have infrastructure challenges. We have political disagreements. You can even build a spectacular roundabout that everyone will complain about for months.  But you cannot manufacture belonging. You cannot pour it into concrete. You cannot buy it from a catalog. MAY ULAN PARIN KAHIT EL NIÑO  Nagbigay ng paalala ang political blogger at commentator na si Atty. Race del Rosario kaugnay ng mga panawagan ng Palasyo na maghanda ang publiko sa inaasahang epekto ng Super El Niño, partikular sa posibleng kakulangan ng suplay ng tubig. Ayon kay Del Rosario, may mga taong maaaring magkamali sa pag-unawa sa Super El Niño at isipin na tuluyan nang mawawala ang ulan. Binigyang-diin niyang hindi nangangahulugan ang pagkakaroon ng El Niño na magiging zero ang pag-ulan sa bansa. Bilang suporta sa kanyang pahayag, binanggit niya ang mga ulat ng Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration (PAGASA) na nagsasaad na maaari pa ring magkaroon ng mga episode ng malakas na pag-ulan kahit sa panahon ng El Niño. “Kaya kung may chance, mag-imbak,” paalala ni Del Rosario, na hinihikayat ang publiko na samantalahin ang pagkakataong makapag-ipon ng tubig kapag may ulan, bilang paghahanda sa mga panahong maaaring bumaba ang suplay nito. Ang kanyang mensahe ay kasabay ng panawagan ng pamahalaan na maghanda sa posibleng epekto ng Super El Niño. Kabilang sa mga hakbang na maaaring gawin ng mga pamilya ang maingat na paggamit ng tubig, pag-iipon nito sa malinis at ligtas na lalagyan, at pag-iwas sa pag-aaksaya. Sa kabila ng posibilidad ng malakas na pag-ulan sa ilang panahon, mahalagang sundin ang mga opisyal na abiso ng PAGASA at mga lokal na awtoridad upang matiyak ang tamang paghahanda sa tagtuyot, pagbaha, at iba pang posibleng epekto ng pabagu-bagong kondisyon ng panahon. #dmlatest

THE HOSTAGE BLUEPRINT: JICA MASTERPLAN FOR DAVAO CITY  What if I told you that a blueprint to stop the flooding in Davao City is already finished? It was designed by some of the best engineers in the world, printed, and is currently sitting on a desk in Manila. Here is the truth about the JICA Master Plan, the political war currently holding it hostage, and what our Local Government Unit (LGU) is doing to keep our heads above water while we wait. The Real Solution: The JICA Master Plan Back in 2018, the Philippine government partnered with the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) to solve our city’s flooding. Instead of just building basic concrete walls (which easily overflow), the Japanese and local engineers designed a massive, city-wide system. The core of the plan involves digging massive "retarding basins" (giant empty catch-ponds built in the uplands). When a storm hits, millions of gallons of water would flow into these basins and be held there safely, trapping the water before it ever reaches barangays like Ma-a, Matina, and Talomo. It is brilliant, it is proven, and it is ready. But just look at the timeline of how it got stuck in politics: Here is the timeline:  April 2019 THE STUDY BEGINS The Philippine government and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) sign an agreement to create a long-term, multi-basin master plan. 2018-2022 WHY WASN’T IT BUILT UNDER DUTERTE? A common question is why this wasn't funded during former President Rodrigo Duterte's term. The answer is engineering reality: The Japanese engineers were still studying our rivers. You cannot fund or construct a mega-project when the architects haven't finished the blueprints. July 2023 THE BLUEPRINT IS FINISHED JICA officially completes the Master Plan. Instead of basic walls, it proposes ₱41.7 Billion to build massive "retarding basins" (giant empty bowls upstream) to catch and hold storm water before it hits our urban barangays. AUGUST 9, 2024 VP SARA CALLS OUT THE MISSING BUDGET Vice President Sara Duterte issues a strong public statement pointing out the lack of government action. She calls out the current administration for refusing to fund the finalized master plan, questioning if the budget is being intentionally withheld simply because the sitting mayor is a Duterte. "Baka naman may alinlangan pa hinggil dito dahil Duterte ang mayor at mas mamarapatin nilang gibain na lang?" she stated. 2025-Present STILL WAITING FOR FUNDS Despite the blueprint being ready for over two years, the national government has still not released the funding needed to actually build it. Bureaucracy or Sabotage? While politicians debate whether the delay is just "standard government red tape" for a foreign loan or a deliberate political attack to damage the Duterte family, ordinary Davaoeños are the collateral damage. We are the ones sweeping mud out of our homes. The ultimate solution to our flooding is being treated as a political football. What is the LGU Doing While We Wait? The Davao City local government cannot afford a ₱41.7 Billion mega-project on its own. They cannot single-handedly buy multi-hectare lands to build giant retarding ponds without national funding. However, they are not just sitting around waiting for our government. Without the big blueprint, the LGU is focusing heavily on immediate urban drainage, nature-based mitigation, and survival. Here is what the city is doing right now:   Aggressive Drainage & Inlet Upgrades: The City Engineer’s Office (CEO) and Task Force Drainage are continuously ripping up flood-prone choke points. In 2025 alone, they funded five new major inlet projects to help water subside faster on critical roads like Diversion Road (fronting Panacan Cemetery), Quezon Boulevard, and Cabantian-Bunawan.  Preventing Blockages: The city’s Ancillary Services Unit (ASU) is conducting aggressive, year-round desilting and garbage clearing of these new drainage systems so the street-level water actually has somewhere to go.   Smart Early Warning Systems: If the LGU cannot completely stop the water, they focus on keeping people alive. Davao City relies heavily on its high-definition river cameras monitoring the Talomo, Matina, and Davao rivers 24/7. This real-time data triggers sirens and preemptive evacuations long before the flood hits living rooms.   Wetlands Protection: The city is pushing for stricter zoning laws to protect remaining natural wetlands and ponding areas from being paved over by commercial developers, allowing nature to absorb some of the rainwater. According to local environmental groups like the Interface Development Intervention for Sustainability (IDIS), Davao City has lost a staggering 95% of its natural wetlands since 1945 due to rapid, unchecked urban development. text: DAVAO FLOODING IS NOT A CORRUPTION ISSUE 1. IT IS a calamity issue - Singapore, the US, Dubai, and other cities also had their fair share of flooding - For Davao, it rained heavily for at least 5 nights, thunderstorms, almost all night. But flooding did not happen until the 4th or 5th night.  This means, of course, the ground is loose, basins are filled, and calamities can occur. - Flooding happened in areas close to the river and low-lying areas, which is a small portion of the whole city. Only 358 families were reported to be affected.  - But for Davao, we had minimal effects. If this had happened elsewhere, it could have been worse. Our LGU learned from the 2011 incident. Our 51-B flood control project protected MILLIONS of us.  2. IT IS NOT a Preparedness-Issue - Unlike other cities, our LGU has a world-class disaster and risk management plan.  - Our 911 is world-class. - Our disaster and rescue facilities and equipment are world-class - Talk about our taxes-well spent - Talk about the years of good governance of the  City Government of Davao - Living in Davao, we feel safe even in calamities, knowing that our LGU will have early warning protocols, search and rescue operations directives, and the PEOPLE OF DAVAO who are there to help each other. - Yes, even if our LGU is there, Davaoeños are also there for the government and for each other. This is why Davao has eagle-like resilience. 3. IT IS NOT a Governance-Issue -  Davao has a working City Social Services and Development Office (CCSDO). It is an exclusive arm of the city to take care of us in case of any fire, flood, or other calamities. - They are seen and felt. They are usually first on the ground to give warm food, clothing, mental health assistance, etc., during disasters. - Baranggay and city officials are mostly on the ground before, during, and after a calamity to facilitate and assist their residents in getting back to its feet. One family at a time, one day at a time. - Suppliers like water,  power, (internet - not so sure), will do their best to restore services asap. OUR CITY OFFICIALS, the Dutertes, are not corrupt and poor in their governance.  This city can withstand trials because we were built to withstand any, YESTERDAY, not when disasters strike. Will calamities hit the city? Big YES! Will we be affected by it?  Also YES! Is our LGU perfect? NO. Is our LGU dependable in times of crisis? Big YES! The effect is not as bad. Because of the last few decades of being raised by the Dutertes, this city is positioned to be forward-thinking. We were able to build this city surge into any economic and natural disaster challenges. So stop bashing the city with its small hit as if it has fallen big time, because even if we were hit, good governance has protected many. This is not like your city, and our experience is not like yours, which shaped your current judgment. And NO, this is not a "zombie-type" and blind following a persona, a name, or a party. Davaoeños are better than that. We will hold our leaders accountable if they mess up.  So stop using a calamity-based hit to shape a political narrative that doesn't exist just to forward an evil notion to destroy credibility and positioning. That's not gonna withstand, because OUR TRUTH is what we experience here daily, backed by YEARS OF GENERALLY A BETTER QUALITY OF LIFE. #davaocity  #raisedbyaduterte   SunStar Davao ,  Davao Today , Ry Llanes,  MindaNews , Kgwd Raymund Carin Gumanid,  GMA Regional TV News Personal Note: Davao is not "better" than other places. Each Philippine city has the potential of achieving better disaster and risk management; the only differentiator is LEADERSHIP. This is why we need to hate corruption and demand accountability from those silencing it; our children deserve a better Philippines.

𝐅𝐨𝐫 𝐀𝐝𝐝𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐈𝐧𝐟𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: The key difference between a 𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐯𝐲 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 and a 𝐖𝐞𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐀𝐝𝐯𝐢𝐬𝐨𝐫𝐲 lies in their forecast period, coverage areas, and accuracy. A 𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐯𝐲 𝐑𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐟𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐖𝐚𝐫𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 provides forecasts for the next three hours and applies up to the municipal level. It is more precise as it utilizes Doppler radar technology to track real-time rainfall intensity, making it highly effective for immediate decision-making in flood-prone areas. House Deputy Speaker and Antipolo City Rep.  Ronnie Puno  backed Senate Blue Ribbon Committee chair  Ping Lacson  in maintaining that there is, so far, no evidence directly linking former Speaker Ferdinand Martin Romualdez to the alleged flood control corruption. Puno said investigations should be guided by evidence and fairness, warning against turning serious allegations into political theater in the absence of proof. He welcomed Lacson’s statement that the Senate inquiry has not produced sworn testimony or documentary evidence implicating Romualdez, adding that investigations cannot proceed on conjecture, political pressure, or unsubstantiated claims. In a radio interview, Lacson said that aside from Orly Guteza, no other witness surfaced to implicate Romualdez in the alleged anomalous flood control projects. Puno also expressed confidence that Lacson could not be pressured or dictated on how to conduct the investigation. House Deputy Speaker and La Union Rep. Paolo Ortega V echoed Lacson’s position and urged critics to stop applying political pressure after the senator said there was no evidence linking Romualdez to the controversy. Ortega said accountability is important but cannot be built on rumors or unsubstantiated claims, adding that the absence of affidavits and documentation leaves no basis for further action. Lanao del Sur Rep. Zia Alonto Adiong likewise welcomed Lacson’s statement, saying that without factual evidence, sworn statements, and supporting documents, there is nothing to pursue. Adiong said the allegations raised by Guteza remain unsubstantiated and warned that manufacturing allegations without evidence undermines due process. He added that public officials are entitled to the same standard of fairness expected of any citizen. While Romualdez’s allies have pointed to the absence of sworn testimony to argue against further proceedings, the Senate inquiry left several matters outside the official record. One unresolved issue involves alleged Romualdez bagman Sofonias “Ponyong” Gabonada, who served as House Deputy Secretary General during Romualdez’s speakership. Gabonada was publicly accused by Davao del Norte Governor Edwin Jubahib of possessing unexplained wealth far beyond what could be justified by his reported ₱200,000 monthly salary as a House official. Jubahib alleged that Gabonada owns a ₱30-million house in Tagum City filled with luxury vehicles, a ₱50-million beach resort in Davao de Oro, and heavy equipment valued at more than ₱200 million. Senator Ronald dela Rosa said during one Senate hearing that Gabonada should be summoned to testify, but Gabonada was never ordered to appear before the Senate. Another aspect of the inquiry involved allegations that members of the so-called Bulacan Group of Contractors (BGC) laundered flood control funds through casinos. In a privilege speech, Lacson cited information obtained from  PAGCOR  regarding large casino transactions allegedly involving the group. Despite these claims, the Lacson-led Blue Ribbon Committee did not summon casino representatives to testify. The hearings did not include sworn testimony from casino operators regarding the alleged use of fake names and IDs or the reported conversion of cash into chips later declared as winnings, as alleged by Lacson. Puno, meanwhile, is a senior leader of the National Unity Party. He previously initiated an ethics complaint against Cavite Rep. Kiko Barzaga, a fellow NUP member and vocal critic of Romualdez, following Barzaga’s public allegations of corruption. “AKALA NAMIN HINDI BINABAHA ANG DAVAO? INIHAMBING DAW SA SINGAPORE?” “Davao is like Singapore daw… ngayon Singapool na?” “Anyare sa Singapore? Mag-sisi na kayo!” Ito ang ilan sa mga komentong kumalat matapos ang pagbaha sa Davao City. Pero bago gawing political weapon ang isang kalamidad, baka kailangan muna nating maintindihan ang totoong nangyari. EDUKASYON MUNA, BAGO PANG-IINSULTO. 1. SINO BA ANG NAGSABING HINDI BINABAHA ANG DAVAO CITY? Walang lungsod sa mundo ang hindi binabaha. Kahit ang mga highly developed cities tulad ng Singapore ay nakakaranas din ng pagbaha. Ang pagiging maunlad ay hindi nangangahulugan na imposibleng tamaan ng kalamidad. Ang Davao City ay hindi simpleng siyudad lamang.  Ito ang pinakamalaking lungsod sa Pilipinas ayon sa lawak ng lupain.  Halos 4 na beses ang lawak ng Metro Manila.  May malawak na kabundukan, watershed areas, ilog, at mabababang lugar. Hindi lahat ng baha ay pare-pareho. 2. BAKIT BINABAHA ANG DAVAO KAHIT MINSAN WALANG MALAKAS NA ULAN SA DOWNTOWN? Dahil ang Davao City ay bahagi ng malalaking river systems. Kasama rito ang:  Lasang River Basin  Bunawan River Basin  Davao River Basin  Matina River Basin  Talomo River Basin  Lipadas River Basin  Sibulan River Basin Ang Davao River at mga tributaries nito tulad ng Panigan at Tamugan Rivers ay nagsisilbing daluyan ng tubig mula sa kabundukan pababa sa Davao Gulf. Kaya kapag malakas ang ulan sa upland areas o kabundukan:  Bababa ang tubig.  Tataas ang water level ng mga ilog.  Maaapektuhan ang low-lying areas. Ito ang tinatawag na upstream runoff. Hindi lahat ng tubig ay galing sa mismong lugar na binaha. 3. HINDI LANG DAVAO ANG BINAGYO NG KALAMIDAD Sa nakalipas na 48 oras:  17 lungsod sa NCR ang naapektuhan ng baha.  6 lungsod sa Region III.  5 lungsod sa Region IV-A.  May mga naapektuhan din sa Region VI, VII, at XII.  At isang lungsod sa Davao Region — ang Davao City. Pero bakit parang Davao lamang ang pinag-uusapan? Bakit ang sakuna ng isang lungsod ay ginagawang pagkakataon para mangutya? 4. ANG BAHA AY HINDI TAGUMPAY NG KAHIT SINONG PANIG Masakit isipin na may ilang taong natuwa sa paghihirap ng iba. May mga nagsasabing “deserve ninyo ‘yan.” Pero kailan naging tama ang pagsasaya sa kalamidad? Ang baha ay hindi pumipili ng kulay ng politika. Hindi nito tinatanong kung sino ang sinusuportahan mo. Kapag may sakuna, ang unang dapat lumabas ay malasakit, hindi pangungutya. 5. OO, MAY KARAPATANG MAGTANONG ANG MGA DABAWENYO Hindi ibig sabihin na ipinagtatanggol ang Davao ay wala nang dapat ayusin. May karapatan ang mga residente na humingi ng:  Mas mahusay na flood control  Mas mabilis na disaster response  Mas matibay na infrastructure  Mas epektibong paghahanda Kung may pagkukulang ang pamahalaan, dapat itong punahin. Ang accountability ay bahagi ng demokrasya. Pero ang pagpuna ay iba sa pang-iinsulto. 6. ANG HINDI NAKIKITA NG IBA: DAVAO KNOWS HOW TO RECOVER Totoo. Nakakatakot ang flash floods. Malakas ang agos. May mga sasakyan at ari-arian na naaapektuhan. Pero isang mahalagang katotohanan: Ang tubig ay mabilis ding humuhupa. Dahil sa natural na topograpiya at daluyan ng mga ilog, matapos dumaan ang malaking volume ng tubig mula sa uplands, mabilis na bumababa ang baha sa maraming lugar. Hindi perpekto ang sistema. Pero hindi rin tama na husgahan ang buong lungsod dahil lamang sa isang kalamidad. 7. ANG DAVAO AY MAY SISTEMA NG PAGHAHANDA Bago pa lumala ang sitwasyon:  May early warning systems.  May monitoring ng water levels.  May rescue operations.  May preemptive evacuations.  Bukas agad ang mga health centers para sa wound care at leptospirosis prevention. Hindi hinihintay ng mga responder na maging huli ang lahat bago kumilos. Sa huli… Maaari tayong magkaiba ng opinyon sa politika. Maaari tayong pumuna. Maaari tayong humingi ng pagbabago. Pero sana huwag nating mawala ang pinakamahalagang bagay: Ang pagiging tao. Ang baha ay hindi dahilan para mawala ang respeto at malasakit sa kapwa Pilipino. Davao will recover. Hindi dahil perpekto ang lungsod. Kundi dahil ang mga Dabawenyo ay sanay humarap sa unos, tumulong sa isa’t isa, at bumangon pagkatapos ng bawat pagsubok. Sa panahon ng kalamidad, hindi dapat lumubog ang ating pagkatao kasama ng baha. DAVAO’S FLOOD MAP EXPLAINED: Why Different Neighborhoods Face Different Flood Risks When heavy rains hit Davao City, why do some neighborhoods experience sudden flash floods that recede in a few hours, while others remain submerged under standing water for days? It all comes down to catchment hydrology. The master plan developed by the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) and the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA) covers 2,200 square kilometers divided into three main river basins. Because each catchment has a unique shape, slope, and size, each one poses a completely different flood threat to specific Davao neighborhoods:  1. Davao River Basin (1,755 km²) — Massive Volume & Standing Water Neighborhoods Affected: Waan, Tigatto, Ma-a, Barangay 19, Barangay 8, and Bucana.  What Happens Here: This is the largest river system in the area. Because its catchment extends deep into the northern mountain ranges, it collects enormous volumes of rainwater. Even when it isn't raining in the downtown area, heavy rainfall up in the mountains eventually travels downstream into the city.  The Engineering Reality: Because the basin is so large, there is a time delay before the main wave of water reaches the city. As the river passes through tight natural bends near Tigatto and Ma-a, the channel gets squeezed, forcing water over the banks. Worse, when peak river flows meet high tides at the river mouth in Bucana, the seawater acts like a natural dam. This creates a severe backwater effect that traps floodwaters inland, causing deep, slow-draining pools that cover over 480 hectares and affect 43,000+ residents.  2. Matina River Basin (70 km²) — Rapid Flash Floods & Highway Bottlenecks  Neighborhoods Affected: Matina Pangi, Gravahan, GSIS Subdivision, and Matina Crossing.  What Happens Here: Unlike the Davao River, Matina suffers from sudden, high-speed flash floods with very little warning time.  The Engineering Reality: This basin is relatively small, steep, and heavily built-up with concrete and asphalt. Because rainwater cannot soak into the ground, it immediately rushes straight into the river channel. Narrow bridge openings—such as the crossing along McArthur Highway—act like narrow bottlenecks. When high-volume runoff reaches these tight spots, the water backs up rapidly and spills sideways over the banks directly into nearby residential subdivisions.  3. Talomo River Basin (204 km²) — Raging Currents & Riverbank Collapse.   Neighborhoods Affected: Talomo Proper, Tugbok, and communities along the Talomo Riverbanks.  What Happens Here: While Talomo does not usually create broad, standing lakes like the Davao River, its waters move at extremely high speeds as they surge down from the slopes of Mount Apo.  The Engineering Reality: The steep drop in elevation gives the rushing water tremendous kinetic energy. Instead of long-term standing pools, the main danger here is high-velocity water scraping against the riverbed and riverbanks. This severe erosion tears away the surrounding land, threatens bridge piers, and causes steep riverbanks to collapse along the Talomo-Tugbok corridor.  4. The "Missing Gaps": Intermediate Basins & Urban Creeks  Neighborhoods Affected: Toril (Lipadas River), Bunawan & Lasang (Bunawan/Licanan Rivers), and Agdao, Bajada & Buhangin (Urban Creek Networks).  The Planning Limitation: On master plan maps, you might notice "uncolored spaces" between the three big basins. In nature, land is continuous—every square meter belongs to a catchment. The JICA study intentionally focused its scope on the three largest high-volume river mains, omitting these smaller intermediate catchments.  Why They Still Matter: These smaller watersheds carry severe flood risk. For instance, the Lipadas River in Toril causes rapid flash evacuations, the Bunawan River frequently submerges portions of the Davao-Agusan Highway, and dense urban creek networks in Agdao and Buhangin overflow quickly during short thunderstorms because over 95% of the city’s natural urban wetlands have been paved over.  Comprehensive city drainage requires addressing these omitted gaps alongside the main rivers.  The Takeaway Whether it’s standing water along the Davao River, flash flooding in Matina, riverbank erosion in Talomo, or creek overflow in Agdao and Toril, any effective flood strategy must treat all catchments as interconnected systems. Dito ba 'yung lugar ni Duterte? Akala namin hindi ito binabaha.   Nakakatawang basahin ang mga komento ng mga hindi taga-rito na ginagawang isyung politikal ang mga pagbaha sa Davao City. Bago ninyo gawing usaping politikal ito, hayaan ninyong ipaliwanag ko ang katotohanang heograpikal tungkol sa mga pagbaha sa Davao City. Bilang isang Dabawenyo mula pagkapanganak, ito ang katotohanang hindi ninyo makikita sa mga viral video na wala sa tamang konteksto. Una, ang Davao City ay isang malaking natural na *catch basin* (tagasalo ng tubig). Hindi lahat ng pagbaha sa Davao ay dahil sa ulan sa mismong lungsod. Kadalasan, matindi ang sikat ng araw sa *downtown* pero binabaha pa rin. Bakit? Dahil sa ulan sa matataas na lugar o agos ng tubig mula sa kabundukan (*mountain runoff*). Matatagpuan ang Davao sa bukana ng malalaking sistema ng ilog. Kapag hindi tumitigil ang ulan sa kabundukan, ang lahat ng tubig doon ay bumabaha at umaapaw patungo sa mga ilog sa ibaba na papunta sa Davao Gulf. Talagang nagsisilbi itong natural na *catch basin* sa ilang bahagi rito. Hindi galing sa ating mga kanal (*drainage*) ang tubig; ito ay agos mula sa bundok na direktang pumapasok sa lungsod. Pangalawa, malakas at mabilis ang agos ng tubig, pero napakabilis din nitong humupa. Totoo, nakakatakot ang mga *flash flood* sa ilang bahagi ng Davao dahil malakas ang agos, kaya may mga sasakyan at bahay na natatangay. Pero ito ang hindi alam ng mga taga-labas: agad na nawawala ang tubig-baha sa Davao. Gaano man kataas ang tubig mula sa bundok, hindi kami binabaha nang ilang araw o linggo. Tinitiyak ng aming *flood control* at topograpiyang mabilis magpatuyo ng tubig na kapag nakalagpas na ang agos mula sa itaas, halos agad na nawawala ang tubig. Panghuli, mayroon kaming *proactive* na pamamahala sa sakuna (*disaster management*). Bago pa man umapaw ang ilog, naka-alerto na ang aming mga *early warning system*. May mga sirena, *recorder*, at sapilitang paglikas (*mandatory evacuation*) na ipinapatupad ng CDRRMO ilang oras bago umabot sa pinakamataas na antas ang tubig. Hindi lang kami basta naghihintay sa baha; pinaghahandaan namin ito. Kaya sa susunod na magkomento kayo, unawain muna ang heograpiya. Ang mga baha sa Davao ay nagmumula sa kabundukan at mabilis na dumadaloy dahil sa *gravity*, ngunit mabilis din itong humuhupa dahil gumagana nang maayos ang *drainage system* ng lungsod. ENGINEERING A FLOOD-RESILIENT DAVAO: A Look into the JICA Flood Control Master Plan Davao City’s rapid urban growth and unique geography make flood management a complex, critical challenge. Tackling water-induced hazards requires more than just reactive measures—it demands a science-backed, basin-wide hydrological strategy. The Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH), in partnership with the Japan International Cooperation Agency (JICA), developed the Master Plan and Feasibility Study on Flood Control and Drainage in Davao City. Here is a bird's-eye view of how this comprehensive framework aims to protect our communities:  1. Broad Scope Across 3 Major Basins Flooding isn't isolated to one river. The master plan covers a massive 2,200 km² target area, addressing three distinct flood types—Riverine, Inland (Urban Drainage), and Coastal—across three key river basins: • Davao River Basin: 1,755 km² • Talomo River Basin: 204 km² • Matina River Basin: 70 km²  2. Structural Interventions (Hard Engineering) To physically manage extreme peak flows during heavy weather events, major infrastructure upgrades are proposed: • Retarding Ponds: Large detention basins to temporarily store stormwater and shave off peak flood flows downstream. • River Dredging: Deepening critical channel beds to maximize volumetric flow capacity. • Cut-off Channels & Floodwalls: Realignment works (including a cut-off-works cum bridge) to bypass tight meanders and safely contain floodwaters. • Urban Drainage Upgrades: Re-engineering internal city networks to prevent localized pooling.  3. Non-Structural Measures (Policy & Preparedness) Infrastructure alone cannot eliminate risk. The plan heavily integrates non-structural controls: • Telemetry & Early Warning: Real-time forecasting systems to provide crucial lead time for communities. • Land-Use & Zoning Controls: Restricting high-density development in active, natural floodplains. • Community Preparedness: Targeted evacuation and safety protocols for vulnerable areas like Bucana, Ma-a, Waan, and Mandug.  4. Geotechnical & Environmental Controls A key engineering hurdle identified is managing the massive volume of excavated silt and soil. Without strict geotechnical protocols—such as temporary siltation ponds and silt curtains—dredging operations risk causing severe downstream sedimentation in the Davao River and Davao Gulf. Engineering long-term flood resilience requires a balance of heavy civil solutions, environmental safeguards, and proactive community planning. BREAKING NEWS: Leptospirosis, itinuturi nang epidemya sa Maynila Itinuturi nang epidemya ang pagdami ng kaso ng leptospirosis sa Lungsod ng Maynila matapos lumagpas sa epidemiologic threshold ang mga naitalang bagong kaso ng naturang sakit.  Sa kanyang ulat kay Manila City Mayor Francisco "Isko" Moreno Domagoso ngayong Lunes ng umaga, sinabi ni Manila OIC-City Health Officer Dr. Grace Padilla na nasa "epidemic condition" na ang pagkalat ng leptospirosis.  Batay sa datos ng Manila Health Department (MHD) na pinamumunuan ni Dr. Padilla, mula sa 1.27% attack rate noong nakaraang linggo, pumalo na ito ngayon sa 3.48%, indikasyon ng mabilis na pagtaas ng kaso sa loob ng maikling panahon.  Dagdag pa ni Dr. Padilla, nasa full capacity na ang ilang city government district hospitals, kabilang ang Ospital ng Maynila, Sta. Ana Hospital at Justice Jose Abad Santos General Hospital dahil sa patuloy na pagdami ng mga pasyente. Sa kanyang direktiba matapos ang ulat ng MHD, inatasan ni Domagoso ang mga ahensya ng Pamahalaang Lungsod na paigtingin ang patuloy na isinasagawang kampanya kontra leptospirosis.  Kabilang dito ang agresibong public information campaign upang maipaalam na mayroong libreng doxycycline capsules sa lahat ng 44 health center at 7 district hospital sa ilalim ng Pamahalaang Lungsod.  Giit ni Domagoso, mabuti nang mismong Pamahalaang Lungsod , sa pamamagitan ng MHD at 896 barangay, ang pumunta sa taumbayan upang mamahagi ng doxycycline sa mga naapektuhan ng pagbaha sa mga nakaraang linggo.  #ManilaPIO   #AlertoManileño

Nanawagan ang dating Davao Responder na si Josephus Christian Serrano sa publiko na seryosohin ang mga utos ng preemptive evacuation upang maiwasan ang panganib sa gitna ng pagbaha. Sa kanyang social media post, sinabi niyang madalas umanong tumatanggi ang ilang residente sa paunang babala ng mga rescuer dahil naniniwalang hindi aabot ang baha sa kanilang lugar. Basahin ang kabuuang mensahe:  "Alam ninyo kung sino ang dapat sisihin. Hindi ko na kailangang sabihin pa. Bakit? Kapag pinapa-preemptive evacuation kayo, ano ang isinasagot ninyo sa mga responder? Lagi ninyong sinasabi, 'Mga sir, malayo pa 'yan. Ilang taon na kaming nakatira rito, hindi na aabot ang baha dito.' Ang isinasagot na lang ng mga responder, 'Kayo na po ang bahala, sir. Basta nabigyan na namin kayo ng babala.' Alam ba ninyo kung bakit alam ng mga responder na may paparating na malaking baha? Dahil maaga pa lang ay may abiso na mula sa mga nasa kabundukan na may malakas na rumaragasang tubig na pababa patungo sa Davao, kaya pinaghahandaan na ito ilang oras bago pa dumating. Pero siyempre, mas naniniwala pa rin kayo sa sarili ninyo. Pagkaraan lang ng ilang oras, bigla nang tumataas ang tubig. Doon na kayo tatawag ng rescue at magpo-post sa social media na humihingi ng tulong. Pinipilit pa ninyo ang mga rescuer na tumawid sa napakalakas na agos ng baha. Akala ba ninyo ay hindi sila maaaring maaksidente? May mga pamilya rin kaming naghihintay na makauwi kaming ligtas. Ano ba naman kung pansamantala muna kayong manatili sa evacuation site nang ilang oras, gayong may pagkain at matutuluyan naman doon. Ginagawa iyon para wala nang kailangang i-rescue. Pagkatapos, saka naman kayo magpo-post na walang silbi ang mga rescuer. Paalala lang ito, lalo na sa mga may mga bata, matatanda, may sakit, persons with disabilities (PWD), at mga buntis sa inyong tahanan. Kung wala pa namang baha, napakadali pang pumunta sa evacuation area. Bakit pa ninyo hihintaying maging napakahirap na kayong ilikas? At bakit mas madali pa kayong maniwala sa mga fake news sa Facebook? Hindi ako galit. Inilalabas ko lang ang nararamdaman ko. Pakibahagi ang mensaheng ito upang makatulong sa pagligtas ng buhay." #LNB
